21.quote_or_event: “The God-conscious being is always unattached, as the lotus in the water remains detached.”
21.explanation: Sukhmani's praise of the brahm giani (God-conscious being) begins with detachment. Unlike the Kural's ascetic, though, the Sikh ideal stays in household life and is detached in the midst of it, like a lotus that sits in water without getting wet.
21.tie_back: Both texts rank highest the person who has let go of desire. Sikhism places that person inside worldly life rather than in renunciation.
21.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 272, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 8, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
21._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong fit on praising freedom from desire, tempered because Sikhism rejects formal renunciation (see Ang 467 on wilderness-dwellers), which the Kural's chapter exalts.

22.quote_or_event: “The God-conscious being cannot be appraised... Who can describe the limits of the God-conscious being? Only the God-conscious being can know the state of the God-conscious being. The God-conscious being has no end or limitation.”
22.explanation: Guru Arjan says again and again that the greatness of the God-conscious person cannot be valued, measured or put into words.
22.tie_back: This is the Kural's own point: trying to measure such greatness is like counting all the dead.
22.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 273, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 8, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
22._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted lines); near one-to-one on immeasurable greatness, though the Sikh figure is a God-conscious householder rather than a renunciant.

23.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, one is happy here and hereafter.”
23.explanation: Sukhmani often pairs this world and the next (halat palat). Spiritual discernment lived out now, in the company of the holy, brings good in both.
23.tie_back: The Kural praises those who have discerned the two orders of existence and live virtuously here and now. This line speaks to the same two worlds and to living them well now.
23.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 272, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 7, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
23._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it matches the 'this world and the next' reading of irumai, but only partially captures the Kural's emphasis on discernment and visible greatness.

24.quote_or_event: “The mind is the elephant, the Guru is the elephant-driver, and knowledge is the whip. Wherever the Guru drives the mind, it goes. O Nanak! Without the whip, the elephant wanders into the wilderness, again and again.”
24.explanation: Guru Amar Das uses the mahout's picture: the mind is a powerful elephant, steered by the Guru with the goad of knowledge.
24.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own image: an elephant held in check by a small goad as the way to the highest state.
24.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 516, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
24._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the elephant-and-goad image is a near one-to-one match, with the difference that the Guru's knowledge, not personal willpower, is the goad, and the mind rather than the five senses is the elephant.

25.quote_or_event: “Ahalyaa was the wife of Gautam the seer. Seeing her, Indra was enticed. When he received a thousand marks of disgrace on his body, then he felt regret in his mind.”
25.explanation: Guru Nanak retells the Puranic story of Indra, who failed to master desire and was disgraced for it. He uses it to show that only those who accept God's hukam stay free of such falls.
25.tie_back: Some commentators, Parimelazhagar among them, read the Kural's Indra as a witness through his fall. Guru Nanak calls Indra up in exactly that role, as proof of what unmastered desire costs.
25.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1344, Raag Prabhati, Dakhni, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
25._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it matches the Ahalya reading of the Kural closely, but not the primary reading of Indra as witness to ascetic power, and Gurbani cites Indra only as a cautionary tale.

26.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. When you place your feet on this Path, give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
26.explanation: Guru Nanak calls the spiritual path the hardest commitment there is: one must be ready to give up one's head and ignore what others think.
26.tie_back: The Kural separates the great from the small by whether they do what is hard. Guru Nanak's path is open only to those willing to do the hardest thing.
26.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
26._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong thematic fit on greatness as willingness to do the hardest thing, though Nanak's verse is an invitation rather than the Kural's two-way definition.

27.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
27.explanation: Guru Nanak recasts the yogi's discipline in inward terms. Whoever masters his own mind has mastered the world, with no need to retreat from it.
27.tie_back: The Kural says the world lies in the grip of whoever understands the five senses. Japji says the world is won by whoever wins his own mind.
27.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib, Pauri 28, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
27._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on inner mastery as mastery of the world, with the mind in place of the five senses.

28.quote_or_event: “The Word, the Bani is Guru, and Guru is the Bani. Within the Bani, the Ambrosial Nectar is contained.”
28.explanation: In Sikhism the Gurus' recorded words are the Guru. That is why Guru Arjan compiled them into the Adi Granth (1604), and why the scripture is honoured today as the living Guru.
28.tie_back: The Kural says the greatness of perfected people is shown by the sacred words they leave behind. Sikhism goes further and treats those words as the Guru's presence itself.
28.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 982, Raag Nat, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
28._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong fit on sacred words as the lasting evidence of the great, though Gurbani identifies the word with the Guru rather than treating it as proof of a person's greatness.

29.quote_or_event: “Slandering the Saints, one’s life is cut short... One who is cursed by a Saint cannot be saved... But if the Compassionate Saint shows His Kindness, O Nanak! In the Company of the Saints, the slanderer may still be saved.”
29.explanation: Guru Arjan warns that wronging a saint brings ruin, and that someone cursed by a saint cannot be saved. He ends by leaving room for the saint's mercy.
29.tie_back: The Kural warns that no one can be shielded from the wrath of those who stand on the hill of character. Sukhmani gives the same warning and adds the saint's power to forgive.
29.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 13, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
29._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipses mark omitted lines); close on the danger of wronging the holy, but Gurbani frames it as the consequence of slander and stresses the saint's mercy, where the Kural stresses the saint's anger.

30.quote_or_event: “Make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, modesty the knot and truth the twist. This is the sacred thread of the soul; if you have it, then go ahead and put it on me.”
30.explanation: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, the boy Nanak refused the Brahmin's sacred thread (janeu). He asked instead for a thread spun from compassion and truth, which cannot break, get dirty or burn.
30.tie_back: Like the Kural's redefinition of anthanar, Guru Nanak redefines the mark of the twice-born as compassion lived out, not birth or ritual.
30.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
30._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on redefining Brahmin status by compassion and conduct, though the Kural's compassion explicitly extends to every living creature.
